High
hī
adj. (elevated in place, rank, or dignity; rendering Hebrew rum, gaboah, elyon, Greek hypsistos)
From Saxon heah, high, tall. In Scripture the word carries a moral charge in both directions: God is the high and lofty One, and the sinner's high look is an abomination — the same height is glory in Him and pride in us.

Biblical Definition

High in Scripture is first a name for God and only afterward a measurement. He is the most High, and the title governs the whole vocabulary of elevation: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). Isaiah gives the fullest statement, and it contains the surprise that keeps the word from becoming mere distance: “For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). The Most High has two addresses, and the second is a broken heart. That is transcendence and condescension held in one verse, and it forbids both the deism that puts God safely above and the sentimentality that brings Him down by lowering Him. In the priesthood the word names the office of the one Mediator: “For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Hebrews 7:26) — separation and exaltation together, since the height is what makes the intercession effectual. Turned toward the creature, high marks the limit of knowledge: “Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it” (Psalm 139:6). And turned toward sin it names idolatry's favourite location, the high places that even good kings failed to remove.

Webster 1828 Definition

Elevated above the surface, and figuratively exalted in rank, dignity, or degree. Scripture makes it a divine title — the most High — while marking the high look and the high place as the standing shapes of pride and idolatry.

expand to see more

HIGH, a. [Sax. heah, heh; G. hoch; D. hoog.] Extending to a great distance above the surface of the earth; elevated; lofty; of great altitude; as a high mountain; a high tower.

2. Elevated in rank, condition, or office; exalted; dignified; as a person of high birth; high in office.

3. Proud; lofty; arrogant; as a high look, which the Scriptures condemn. Prov. 21.

4. Great in degree or intensity; as high winds; high esteem; a high price.

5. Applied to the Supreme Being, the most High, denoting his supremacy over all created things. He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High. Ps. 91. Also, the high places, the elevated spots where idolatrous worship was performed.

Key Scripture

Psalm 91:1 — "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."

Isaiah 57:15 — "For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones."

Hebrews 7:26 — "For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens;"

Psalm 139:6 — "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it."

Modern Corruption

The height of God has been flattened into friendliness — a God near at hand and nothing else — so that Isaiah's pairing of the high and holy place with the contrite heart is halved, and only the comfortable half is preached.

expand to see more

A generation taught to speak of God chiefly as friend, companion, and the one who is with us has kept a true thing and lost the thing that made it staggering. Isaiah 57:15 does not begin with nearness; it begins with the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy, and only then adds the second dwelling. Remove the first clause and the second is no longer grace, merely proximity — a God who is near because He was never far, never holy, never a consuming fire. The practical effects are visible in worship that cannot produce reverence, in prayer that has lost the posture of a suppliant, and in a doctrine of sin that cannot explain why a contrite spirit was necessary in the first place. Psalm 139:6 belongs here too: a God whose knowledge is too high for the creature to attain is not a God the creature may edit.

The opposite failure has its own history in Scripture, and the high places are its monument. Israel did not usually abandon the LORD outright; she worshipped Him, and then also kept the elevated shrines, and the historian's refrain over one decent king after another is that the high places were not taken away. That is the enduring pattern of half-reformation: real repentance in the centre, an unrelinquished altar on the hill. The principle to recover is that height belongs to God alone — He is the most High, and every rival elevation, whether a hilltop shrine or a private reservation in the heart, is to be pulled down rather than tolerated. Where the true height is confessed, the false ones lose their attraction; where it is softened, they multiply.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew elyon (Most High), rum (to be high, lifted up), gaboah (lofty, haughty), and bamah (high place); Greek hypsistos (highest) and hypsos (height, exaltation).

expand to see more

Hebrew elyon (H5945) — Most High; the divine title in Psalm 91:1 and in Melchizedek's priesthood of the most high God.

Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, rise, be lifted up; used of God's exaltation and of the proud high look.

Hebrew gaboah (H1364) — high, lofty, and by extension haughty; the word in “the high and lofty One” register.

Hebrew bamah (H1116) — high place; the elevated shrine repeatedly said not to have been taken away.

Greek hypsistos (G5310) — highest, most high; the title in “Glory to God in the highest” and in the Son of the Highest.

Usage

"“The secret place of the most High” — the title of supremacy used as the address of refuge."

"“I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” — two dwellings, one God."

"“It is high, I cannot attain unto it” — the creature confessing the ceiling of his own knowledge."
